title: Beshalach: held-up hands (Exodus 17:8–13)
hookLine: when Moses' arms tire, Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset

cards: Hold your arms straight out in front of you. Not for a few seconds; for a minute. Then imagine an afternoon.

The shoulders burn first, then the forearms shake, and at some point the arms just drop, no matter how much you care. The Israelites are camped at a place called Rephidim when a people called Amalek attacks them.
Joshua leads the fighters below. Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand. And the battle comes down to something as ordinary and human as tired arms.

teach.b: When Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails. When he lets them down, Amalek prevails. And his hands get heavy.
So two people step in: Aaron, his brother, and Hur, a man we barely meet anywhere else.

teach.h: AARON AND HUR, ONE ON EACH SIDE.
teach.b: They put a stone under Moses so he can sit, and they stand one on each side holding up his arms, "and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun."
The word for steady, emunah, is the word usually translated faith. His hands were faithfulness, held up by friends. The Mishnah asks the obvious question: did Moses' hands win or lose a war?
When Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven, they prevailed; when they didn't, they fell. The hands were a sign pointing up.
The Talmud notices the stone. Why not a cushion? Because Moses wouldn't sit in comfort while his people were suffering in the fight.
And Amalek becomes a name in Jewish memory. Deuteronomy says they struck at the weary and the stragglers at the rear, and in tradition Amalek comes to stand for cruelty that targets the weak.
So Beshalach ends where it began, with a people learning to walk: the long way round, Joseph's bones, the sea, bitter water, and now Moses on a hill, held up by friends.

how: The Amalek story is read in synagogue on the morning of Purim, since Haman is traditionally linked to Amalek, and on the Shabbat before Purim the command to remember Amalek is read from Deuteronomy.

games.q: you're Aaron. the battle depends on Moses' raised hands, and his arms are shaking. what do you do?
o: take the staff and hold it yourself.
sit him on a stone and hold up his arms with Hur.
games.why: a stone under him, one friend on each side, and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.

practice: If you can, lift your arms a little and feel how soon they want to fall, then rest them. Think of someone holding something up all day, a parent caring for a child or an aging mother, a teacher, a nurse, a friend carrying a cause.
Picture standing beside them like Aaron, or like Hur, and ask what holding up their arms would look like.

wordCard.voice: Amalek. The people who attacked Israel at Rephidim, striking at the weary, and the battle won while friends held up Moses' tired hands.

orig.note: Hebrew: Amalek, the people who attacked at Rephidim; in tradition, a name for cruelty to the weak.

carryVoice: Your line: hold up the hands. Nobody is meant to hold them up alone. Until tomorrow.
